name: Contraception
tagline: Your options. What's free. What suits your life.

what_is_it.heading: Contraception in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Contraception lets you choose when and if you have children. South Africa offers a wide range of methods — most are free at government clinics. Different methods suit different lives.
paragraphs: There is no 'best' method — only the best for you right now. Choices depend on your age, health, plans for children, partner situation, and lifestyle. The right method is one you'll actually use consistently.

All government clinics provide contraception free of charge. You don't need to involve your partner, parents (from age 12), or anyone else. Confidentiality is protected by South African law — healthcare workers cannot share your contraceptive choices without your permission.

items.headline: All free
items.body: Pills, injections, implants, IUDs, condoms — all available free at every government clinic.

items.headline: Many options
items.body: Daily pills, monthly injections, 3-monthly injections, implants lasting 3 years, IUDs lasting up to 10 years.

items.headline: Confidential
items.body: From age 12 you can access contraception privately. Healthcare workers cannot tell parents or partners without your permission.

items.headline: Emergency pill
items.body: Morning-after pill works up to 5 days after sex — but the sooner the better. Free at clinics, available at most pharmacies.

pull_quote.text: Only condoms protect against both pregnancy AND STIs. Hormonal methods are highly effective for pregnancy but offer no protection from infections. Double up if you can.

signs.heading: Which method fits your life?
signs.lede: There's no single right answer. Match the method to your life — and remember you can switch any time.

items.title: Want long-term, low-effort
items.description: Implant (3 years, small rod in upper arm) or IUD (3–10 years depending on type). Both are highly effective and you can forget about them once in place.

items.title: Want monthly control
items.description: Pill (taken daily at the same time) or injection (monthly or 3-monthly). Good if you may want pregnancy in the next year or two.

items.title: Want STI protection too
items.description: Male or female condoms — every time, with or without other contraception. Only these protect against HIV and STIs.

myths.heading: What is true and what is not

items.fact: All reversible methods let your fertility return after stopping — usually within months. There is no long-term effect on having children later when you want them.

items.myth: You can't get pregnant on your first time, or while breastfeeding.
items.fact: You absolutely can. Always use contraception if you don't want pregnancy — first time, period, or any time after birth.

items.myth: The pill protects against HIV and STIs.
items.fact: Hormonal contraception prevents pregnancy only. For STIs and HIV — condoms every time, or PrEP if at higher HIV risk.

items.myth: Emergency contraception is the same as abortion.
items.fact: Emergency contraception works before pregnancy starts — it delays ovulation. It cannot end an existing pregnancy. Termination of pregnancy is a separate, legal service.

items.title: Go to any government clinic
items.description: Walk in. Ask for contraception. They'll explain options and help you choose. No appointment needed, no medical aid required.

items.title: Try a method — and switch if it doesn't fit
items.description: Side effects with one method don't mean others will give you problems. Many women try 2 or 3 before finding the right one. Switching is free.

items.title: If you miss a pill — check the leaflet
items.description: Different pills have different rules. Generally: take the missed pill as soon as you remember, and use condoms for 7 days as backup.

items.title: If sex without protection happens
items.description: Emergency contraception within 5 days. Free at clinics. R30–80 at most pharmacies. The sooner the better. Doesn't replace regular contraception.

items.title: Couples — try to decide together
items.description: Contraception works best when both partners support the choice. Many clinics offer couples counselling. Outcomes are better when you're on the same page.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Contraception is one of South Africa's best-organised public health services. Free, confidential, available to everyone from age 12.

helplines.name: Find your nearest clinic
helplines.description: Every government clinic provides free contraception and counselling
helplines.meta: No appointment · no medical aid required · age 12+
